source_text: Ὅλως γὰρ οὐδ᾽ εὐσεβεῖν εἰς τῶν ὅλων δεσπότην, τοῦτο ὃ δὴ μόνος τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς πάντων ζώων ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἔχειν ἐτιμήθη τε καὶ ἠξιώθη, καὶ εἰκότως πᾶς ὁστισοῦν καὶ σοφὸς καὶ ἀμαθὴς, περιέχεται τούτου, ὅστις μὴ παντελῶς τὰς ἐννοίας ἀπολώλεκεν ὑπό τινος φρενοβλαβείας. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ εὐσεβεῖν ὅλως δυνατὸν εἶναι ἔφασκεν, ὀρθῶς λέγων, μὴ φιλοσοφήσαντι. ἕως πολλοὺς τοιούτους ἄλλους ἐπ᾽ ἄλλοις ἐπαντλῶν λόγους, ὥσπερ τινὰς καταγεγοητευμένους ἐπὶ τέλει ταῖς αὐτοῦ τέχναις ἀκινήτους ἀτεχνῶς, φέρων ἡμᾶς παρεδρύσατο, λόγοις τοῖς αὐτοῦ, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως σύν τινι θείᾳ δυνάμει. καὶ γὰρ καὶ φιλίας ἡμῖν κέντρον ἐνέσκηψεν, οὐκ εὐκαταγώνιστόν τι, δριμὺ δὲ καὶ ἀνυτικώτατον, δεξιότητος καὶ διαθέσεως τῆς ἀγαθῆς, ὅση εὐνοητική τις ἡμῖν αὐταῖς φωναῖς αὐτοῦ προσφθεγγομένου καὶ ὁμιλοῦντος, ἐνεφαίνετο. οὐκ ἐκπεριεῖναι ἡμᾶς ἄλλως λόγοις πειρωμένου, δεξιᾷ δὲ καὶ φιλανθρώπῳ καὶ χρηστοτάτῃ γνώμῃ σώζειν τε καὶ κοινωνοὺς τῶν τε ἐκ φιλοσοφίας ἀγαθῶν καταστήσασθαι, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων μάλιστα ὅσα τὸ θεῖον παρὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς εἰ καὶ παρὰ πάντας ἴσως τοὺς νῦν ἀνθρώπους, αὐτῷ μόνῳ ἐδωρήσατο· τὸν διδάσκαλον εὐσεβείας, τὸν σωτήριον λόγον, πολλοῖς μὲν ἐπιφοιτῶντα, καὶ πάντας κατεργαζόμενον ὅσοις ἂν προστύχῃ· οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ὅτι αὐτῷ ἐνστήσεται, πάντων καὶ ὄντι καὶ ἐσομένῳ βασιλεῖ. κρυπτόμενον δὲ, καὶ οὐ γνωριζόμενον οὔτε ῥᾳδίως οὔτε δυσχερῶς τοῖς πολλοῖς, ὡς ἐρωτηθέντας ἔχειν περὶ αὐτοῦ σαφὲς εἰπεῖν.
thought_title: No true piety without philosophy; the sting of friendship
orientation: Origen teaches that there is no true piety without philosophy, and his words strike like a goad.
pass_a_gloss: For on the whole, not even to be pious (eusebein) toward the Master (despotes) of all things, this which alone of all living things (zoa) on earth man was honored (etimethe) and counted worthy (exiothe) to have, and which reasonably everyone whosoever, both wise and ignorant, holds to (periechetai), whoever has not wholly lost his notions (ennoiai) through some derangement (phrenoblabeia): not then even to be pious at all is possible, he kept saying (ephasken), speaking rightly, for one not having philosophized (philosophesanti). Until, pouring on (epantlon) many other such words upon others, as though bewitched (katagegoeteumenous) at the end by his arts (technai), simply unmoved (akinetous), bearing us he seated us beside [him] (paredrysato), by his words, I know not how, with some divine power (theia dynamis). For he also hurled into us (eneskepsen) a goad (kentron) of friendship (philia), not easily fought down (eukatagoniston), but sharp (drimy) and most effective (anytikotaton): of dexterity (dexiotes) and good disposition (diathesis), as much as appeared (enephaineto) benevolent (eunoetike) toward us in his very words as he addressed and conversed (homilountos) with us. Not trying otherwise by words to get round (ekperieinai) us, but by a kindly (dexia) and humane (philanthropos) and most good (chrestotate) intention (gnome) to save and to make sharers (koinonoi) of the goods from philosophy, and most of all of the others, as many as the divine (to theion) gave to him alone beyond the many, if not perhaps beyond all men now: the teacher (didaskalos) of piety (eusebeia), the saving Word (soterios logos), visiting (epiphoitonta) many and subduing (katergazomenon) all whom it may meet; for there is nothing that will stand against (enstesetai) him, being and going to be King (basileus) of all. But hidden (kryptomenon), and not recognized (gnorizomenon) either easily or with difficulty (dyscheros) by the many, so as, being asked, to be able to say anything clear about it.

pass_b_english: For he said, and rightly, that no one who has not practiced philosophy can be pious at all toward the Master of all. Piety is something that human beings alone, of all living creatures on earth, have been honored and judged worthy to possess; and with good reason every person, wise or ignorant, holds fast to it, unless he has lost his notions entirely through some derangement of mind. So he went on, pouring out one such argument after another, until at last, as if we were spellbound by his arts, he carried us and set us down beside him, simply unable to move, by his words and, I do not know how, with some divine power.

For he also drove into us the sting of friendship, not easy to fight off, but sharp and most effective: the sting of his kindness and good disposition, the goodwill toward us that showed in the very words he used as he spoke and talked with us. He was not trying merely to get the better of us with arguments. With a kindly, humane, and most generous purpose, he sought to save us and to make us sharers in the goods that come from philosophy, and most of all in those others which God had given to him alone above the many, perhaps even above everyone now living: the teacher of piety, the saving Word. That Word comes to many and overcomes all whom it meets, for nothing will stand against the One who is, and will be, King of all. Yet the Word is hidden, and most people do not come to know it, whether easily or with difficulty, well enough to say anything clear about it when asked.
notes: The first sentence is an anacoluthon in the Greek (Gregory begins, breaks off for a relative clause about piety, then restarts with 'ou toinyn oude eusebein'); the English states the claim once and then gives the relative clause as its own sentence. The print has 'eis ton holon despoten' with the article missing before despoten; the sense ('the Master of all') is clear. Doubtful readings: 'anytikotaton' (most effective) and 'ekperieinai' (to get round, overcome) were checked on the page image (PDF p. 83) and stand as printed; Koetschau agrees. 'Whether easily or with difficulty': the print reads 'oute rhadios oute dyscheros' (PDF p. 84, checked on the page image; Koetschau 'oute kai dyscheros'). 'God' renders to theion (the Divine), which here means God. 'The teacher of piety, the saving Word' stands in apposition to 'those others' that God gave to Origen; the Word is capitalized as the divine Logos, and 'the One who is, and will be, King of all' refers to the same Word. 'Kentron' is rendered 'sting' (goad), as in the source title. No Scripture is quoted; 'King of all' and the Word that nothing withstands are left uncited.
